# Learn a topic properly before you explain it

This feature helps you or your team actually understand a decision, a feature or a piece of work, instead of just skimming it. It turns the existing notes and history on a task into a short written explanation, then checks your understanding with questions, so the knowledge sticks rather than fades.

## Contents

- [What it does for you](#what-it-does-for-you)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Good to know](#good-to-know)
- [Words used here](#words-used-here)

## What it does for you

- Pulls together everything already known about a topic, the reasoning, the alternatives considered, the risks, and where it lives in the work, into one clear write-up.
- Only states things that are backed by the existing records, and openly says when a reason was never written down.
- Quizzes you one question at a time and tells you if your answer was complete, partial, or missing something, with a pointer to the missing piece.
- Keeps track of how well you know each topic, so the next time you study it, it starts with what you got wrong before.
- Flags what has changed since you last studied a topic, so you are not caught out by updates.

## How it works

1. You ask to study a topic, for example a specific task or decision.
2. You get a written study note covering what it is, why it was done, how it works, the roads not taken, and the risks.
3. You are quizzed one question at a time, and you answer first.
4. You are told whether each answer was complete, partial, or missing, with the missing part shown.
5. Your score and weak spots are saved against the topic.
6. Next time you study the same topic, the weak questions come first and you are shown what changed in the meantime.

## Good to know

- If the underlying records never explained a reason, the study note will say so rather than guessing.
- If something is found missing from the written material, it gets turned into a follow-up task rather than silently ignored.
- Studies cited by the team suggest that asking questions and getting explained to leads to much better retention than simply having work done for you, which is the thinking behind this feature.

## Words used here

- task: a unit of work that notes, decisions and questions can be attached to.
- agent: the assistant that writes the study note and asks the questions.
